key_claims: β-arrestin2 deficiency produces sexually dimorphic effects on Aβ pathology, neuroinflammation, cognition, and autophagic flux in APP/PS1 mice.
In males, Arrb2 deletion reduced Aβ oligomer burden, enhanced autophagy, suppressed astrocytic and microglial reactivity, and broadly rescued cognition.
In females, Aβ pathology and astrogliosis were unchanged, microgliosis was enhanced, and cognitive improvement was limited to recognition memory.
The male-specific reduction in pathology was accompanied by decreased S473-Akt and S9-GSK3β phosphorylation and enhanced GSK3β/ZBTB16-mediated autophagy.
β-arrestin2 is identified as a sex-dependent node linking Aβ pathology to cognitive outcomes in males but not females.
limitations: The study is based on a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease (APP/PS1), which may not fully recapitulate human disease.
The findings are specific to β-arrestin2 deficiency and may not generalize to other interventions or models.
The molecular mechanisms are described in the context of the study but may not be fully understood.
The study does not provide direct evidence in humans.
what_not_to_say: Do not claim that β-arrestin2 is a therapeutic target for Alzheimer's disease in humans.
Do not state that β-arrestin2 deficiency is beneficial or harmful in humans.
Do not generalize the findings to all Alzheimer's disease patients or to both sexes equally.
Do not claim that the study proves a causal relationship between β-arrestin2 and Alzheimer's disease.
